title: Relative Clauses: Who, Which, That, Whose, Where
learningObjectives: Understand the difference between defining and non-defining relative clauses
Use who, which, that, whose, and where correctly
Know when to use commas with relative clauses
Identify when the relative pronoun can be omitted

sections.title: What Are Relative Clauses?
sections.content: Relative clauses give us extra information about a noun. They act like adjectives — they describe or identify which person or thing we're talking about. Understanding relative clauses will make your English more natural and your sentences more complex and connected.

sections.title: Defining Relative Clauses
sections.content:
<Defining relative clauses> tell us which person/thing we mean. Essential to the sentence.

• <who> (people): The woman <who> lives next door is a doctor.
• <which> (things): The book <which> you recommended is excellent.
• <that> (informal, people/things): The car <that> he bought is red.
• <whose> (possession): The student <whose> laptop was stolen reported it.
• <where> (places): The restaurant <where> we had dinner is closing.

No commas — the clause is essential to the meaning.

sections.title: Non-Defining Relative Clauses
sections.content:
<Non-defining relative clauses> add extra (non-essential) information. Rules:
• Use COMMAS: My sister, <who> lives in London, is visiting.
• NEVER use <that>: Paris, <which> is the capital of France, is beautiful.

• My car, <which> I bought last year, has broken down.
• Tom, <whose> father is a pilot, wants to fly.
• Barcelona, <where> I spent my holiday, is fascinating.

Compare: The students who passed celebrated. (WHICH ones?) vs The students, who studied hard, passed. (ALL)

sections.title: When Can We Omit the Relative Pronoun?
sections.content:
In <defining> clauses, we can omit <who>/<which>/<that> when they are the OBJECT (not subject).

Object — can omit:
• The film (that) we watched was boring. ← 'we' is subject
• The man (who) I met yesterday is my cousin.

Subject — cannot omit:
• The woman who called you is my boss. ← 'who' is the subject
• The train which arrives at 9 is always late.

Tip: If another subject follows the relative pronoun, you can omit it.

sections.title: More Examples in Context
sections.content:
Example 1: DEFINING - <The people who work in that office are very friendly.>

Example 2: NON-DEFINING - <My phone, which I only bought last month, is already crashing.>

Example 3: OMISSION - <The cake you made was delicious.> (omitted 'that/which')

Example 4: WHOSE - <I know a woman whose son won the competition.>

sections.title: Key Points to Remember
sections.content:
1. Defining = essential info, no commas, can use 'that'
2. Non-defining = extra info, with commas, NEVER 'that'
3. Who = people, which = things, whose = possession, where = places
4. You can omit the pronoun when it's the object (not subject) of a defining clause
5. Practice identifying whether information is essential (defining) or extra (non-defining)

keyVocabulary.definition: A clause that gives information about a noun, introduced by who/which/that/whose/where
keyVocabulary.example: The man who called is my uncle.

keyVocabulary.definition: Essential information that identifies which noun we mean
keyVocabulary.example: The book that I need is on the shelf.

keyVocabulary.definition: Extra, non-essential information added between commas
keyVocabulary.example: My car, which is blue, is parked outside.

keyVocabulary.definition: Words like who, which, that, whose, where used to introduce relative clauses
keyVocabulary.example: She's the teacher whose classes are always full.

keyVocabulary.definition: To leave out or not include something
keyVocabulary.example: You can omit 'that' when it's the object.

grammarPoints.explanation: Defining = no commas, essential. Non-defining = commas, extra info.
examples: The car that I want is expensive.

grammarPoints.explanation: Omit who/which/that only in defining clauses when the pronoun is the object.
examples: The film (that) we saw was great.
commonMistakes: Omitting the pronoun when it's the subject
